I am completely bamboozled by the following thing. I have two instances i1 and i2 of type Ring X, and they're equal with reducible_and_instances. Furthermore, when I check this, it is fast.

However, if I do the same check with i1.toAddGroupWithOne and i2.toAddGroupWithOne, both of type AddGroupWithOne X, they're still equal with reducible_and_instances, but when I check this, Lean unfolds everything and the check takes 30x as long. This leads to nontrivial slowdowns and timeouts in FLT.

Here's the example.

import Mathlib.RingTheory.Valuation.Discrete.Basic

open IsDedekindDomain HeightOneSpectrum

variable (A K : Type*) [CommRing A] [Field K]
    [Algebra A K] [IsFractionRing A K] [IsDedekindDomain A]
    (v : HeightOneSpectrum A)

example :
    (WithVal.instField (valuation K v)).toDivisionRing.toRing =
    (WithVal.instRing (valuation K v)) := by
  with_reducible_and_instances rfl -- fast

example :
    (WithVal.instField (valuation K v)).toDivisionRing.toRing.toAddGroupWithOne =
    (WithVal.instRing (valuation K v)).toAddGroupWithOne := by
  with_reducible_and_instances rfl -- slow

Here "fast" and "slow" are relative: in fact the "slow" thing is fast, but the "fast" thing is instantaneous. If you look at the the profiler trace then you can see why -- the moment you start unfolding them you have many fields which you need to check are equal, and this might lead to more unfolding etc etc.

I am really surprised that typeclass inference will check i1 = i2 without unfolding, but unfolds when checking i1.toAddGroupWithOne = i2.toAddGroupWithOne. This is happening everywhere in various valuation files, both in mathlib and in FLT.

Here's the same code again but with the traces included, so you can see the 30x slowdown and what exactly is going on. The defeq check goes from 6329 heartbeats to 182980.

I'm on commit from about half an hour ago. By "slow" I mean "30x slower than the instantaneous one". The "slow" declaration compiles in 0.016 seconds on my machine. The issue isn't this specific example, it is "why the heck is everything unfolding".
On the playground, I see exactly the same time for the two instances, that's why I am confused.
(With heartbeats instead of times, I can see the difference, but it's a factor of x2, not x30)
I think the reason is that AddGroupWithOne is not a direct parent of Ring, so Lean has to unfold and repack stuff to compare the two instances.

You can see the same here

import Mathlib

variable (K : Type*)

def L := K

instance instLField [Field K] : Field (L K) := inferInstanceAs (Field K)
instance instLRing [Ring K] : Ring (L K) := inferInstanceAs (Ring K)

variable [Field K]

set_option trace.profiler.useHeartbeats true
set_option trace.profiler true

example : (instLField K).toDivisionRing.toRing = instLRing K := by
  with_reducible_and_instances rfl --78301 heartbeats

example : (instLField K).toDivisionRing.toRing.toAddGroupWithOne =
    (instLRing K).toAddGroupWithOne := by
  with_reducible_and_instances rfl --142281 heartbeats

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

(With heartbeats instead of times, I can see the difference, but it's a factor of x2, not x30)

Yes, that's because [definition.header] takes the same amount of time (in both cases) as the slow [definition.value]. It's only [definition.value] which is 30x quicker. In the spoiler I showed exactly which part of the trace is problematic. Your 2x observation is because N+N is 2x as big as N+(N/30).

Riccardo -- thanks for the minimisation! Indeed this is the same phenomenon. The Meta.isDefEq check in [definition.value] goes from 7543 in the fast case to 55003 in the slow case, again because of the explosion in the slow case

In the slow case you are paying 7500 (the speed that you can check two instances are defeq without unfolding) but paying it many times: zsmul, IntCast, NatCast, AddMonoid, AddCommMonoid, One, Neg and Sub.

(and in the FLT example this is a lot more expensive, because the instances are both on type synonyms which are now one-field structures after 4.29 encouraged us to do this; the change was made in #34049, so there is a lot of passing around equivalences)
This seems the old discussion about flat structures vs non-flat ones. Maybe @Eric Wieser has something to say.
Well, this problem would not be solved if we had flat structures, right?
We would be able to play more with how instances are defined (I think), but I was didn't mean flat structures are the solution, just that this happens because we have preferred parents.

I think it might be more fair to say that this happens because of a limitation in the unification algorithm. Because with normal function applications, e.g. f a =?= f b, unification will try to unify a =?= b before trying to unfold f. But aparently, it doesn't do that for instance projections.
Ah good point! I was trying to clarify in my head why human beings don't struggle with this but it was so trivial I didn't find the words, and it is exactly what you are saying.
I don't mean to say that adding this extra step to the algorithm will simply make everything work. It probably will give a lot of slowdowns too. But it's certainly something to consider.

I haven't got #38017 to compile yet (and I am leaving it for this evening) but does anyone have a comment on its slightly nonstandard approach?

attribute [-instance] Ring.toAddGroupWithOne

instance Ring.toAddGroupWithOne' (R : Type u) [Ring R] : AddGroupWithOne R :=
  @AddGroupWithOne.mk R Ring.toIntCast inferInstance inferInstance
    inferInstance Ring.sub_eq_add_neg Ring.zsmul Ring.zsmul_zero' Ring.zsmul_succ'
    Ring.zsmul_neg' Ring.neg_add_cancel intCast_ofNat intCast_negSucc

I am making Ring.toAddGroupWithOne' a "fast instance" manually. It solves the problem upthread but I don't know what other damage it may cause. Right now it's broken a random number field file :-/
Repeating my comment from the PR, attribute [-instance] doesn't really do anything (or at least, should be read as as attribute [-instance] ... in)

Related: does anyone understand our choices for the "preferred parent"? Example:

class AddGroupWithOne (R : Type u) extends IntCast R, AddMonoidWithOne R, AddGroup R where

Why is IntCast the "preferred parent" for AddGroupWithOne? Another approach I considered was simply changing the definition so that AddGroup was the prefered parent (and making other similar changes).

Re attribute [-instance] I guess that whether or not it does anything, making the second instance Ring.toAddGroupWithOne' will ensure that the instance Ring.toAddGroupWithOne never fires (unless someone changes a priority later on).
I don't understand how Ring.toAddGroupWithOne' is any better or faster than Ring.toAddGroupWithOne. Aren't they just the same thing?

For the order in which parents appear in the extends clause, the order only matters between classes that have an overlap. So because IntCast doesn't overlap with the other two classes, you can ignore it in the consideration. The only relevant choice is about whether AddMonoidWithOne or AddGroup is the more preferred parent.

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

Aren't they just the same thing?

Kevin's version has extra inferInstance wrappers, for one
But replacing those with delta%, the answer is still yes

You can see the effect of reordering extends classes by looking at the generated .mk constructor. Changing the position of IntCast should only change the order of arguments of .mk. But swapping AddMonoidWithOne and AddGroup will actually change the arguments of .mk.

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

I don't understand how Ring.toAddGroupWithOne' is any better or faster than Ring.toAddGroupWithOne. Aren't they just the same thing?

Well this is strange because experts are telling me they're the same thing, but I thought I checked that they were fixing the unfolding problem upthread? (I need to sleep now unfortunately)

Without the inferInstances, the generated one is

def Ring.toAddGroupWithOne.{u} : {R : Type u} → [self : Ring R] → AddGroupWithOne R :=
fun R self =>
  @AddGroupWithOne.mk R (@Ring.toIntCast R self)
    (@AddMonoidWithOne.mk R (@Semiring.toNatCast R (@Ring.toSemiring R self))
      (@AddCommMonoid.toAddMonoid R
        (@NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring.toAddCommMonoid R
          (@NonUnitalSemiring.toNonUnitalNonAssocSemiring R
            (@Semiring.toNonUnitalSemiring R (@Ring.toSemiring R self)))))
      (@Semiring.toOne R (@Ring.toSemiring R self)) ⋯ ⋯)
    (@Ring.toNeg R self) (@Ring.toSub R self) ⋯ (@Ring.zsmul R self) ⋯ ⋯ ⋯ ⋯ ⋯ ⋯

and Kevin's is

def Ring.toAddGroupWithOne'.{u} : (R : Type u) → [self : Ring R] → AddGroupWithOne R :=
fun R [self : Ring R] =>
  @AddGroupWithOne.mk R (@Ring.toIntCast R self)
    (@AddCommMonoidWithOne.toAddMonoidWithOne R
      (@NonAssocSemiring.toAddCommMonoidWithOne R (@Semiring.toNonAssocSemiring R (@Ring.toSemiring R self))))
    (@SubNegMonoid.toNeg R (@AddGroup.toSubNegMonoid R (@AddCommGroup.toAddGroup R (@Ring.toAddCommGroup R self))))
    (@SubNegMonoid.toSub R (@AddGroup.toSubNegMonoid R (@AddCommGroup.toAddGroup R (@Ring.toAddCommGroup R self)))) ⋯
    (@Ring.zsmul R self) ⋯ ⋯ ⋯ ⋯ ⋯ ⋯
The difference is that when using extends A, B, C, the non-preferred instances for C is not constructed in terms of the one for B, whereas Kevin's is
I think that's maybe ok, but it does seem like a bug that the instance for C is not constructed in terms of the one for the preferred A
Does class Ring (R : Type u) extends Semiring R, AddCommGroupWithOne R make things better here?
Wait, why was it never that in the first place? I don't particularly expect this change to help, but it seems like a more sensible definition
I think it was less performant in some lean version
You could argue that should actually be class Ring (R : Type u) extends Semiring R, NonAssocRing R, NonUnitalRing R
CommRing is similarly weird

Eric Wieser said:

You could argue that should actually be class Ring (R : Type u) extends Semiring R, NonAssocRing R, NonUnitalRing R

I just tried this in #38043 and the result is not very good (+0.43%).
What if you fix CommRing at the same time?
What fix do you imagine?
extends Ring, NonUnitalCommRing, CommSemiring, NonAssocCommRing or similar
Also, the PR you link above does not make the change I suggested in the message you quote.
The PR has several experiments, so the last version is not the suggested change but one of the previous versions is, and you can see that outcome of the radar there.

So I've tried several things in #38043.

class Ring (R : Type u) extends Semiring R, NonAssocRing R, NonUnitalRing R

is slower by 0.43%.

class Ring (R : Type u) extends Semiring R, AddCommGroupWithOne R

is slower by 0.26%.

And keeping the current definitions but using Kevin's formula, i.e.

attribute [instance 0] Ring.toAddGroupWithOne

instance Ring.toAddGroupWithOne' (R : Type u) [Ring R] : AddGroupWithOne R :=
  @AddGroupWithOne.mk R Ring.toIntCast inferInstance inferInstance
    inferInstance Ring.sub_eq_add_neg Ring.zsmul Ring.zsmul_zero' Ring.zsmul_succ'
    Ring.zsmul_neg' Ring.neg_add_cancel intCast_ofNat intCast_negSucc

is slower by 0.12%.

I previously experimented with some adjustments in #7873 before decoupling the algebra and the order hierarchy. I wanted to revisit this after decoupling the algebra and the normed hierarchy, but it has never been resolved.

Sébastien Gouëzel tried to decouple the algebra and norm hierarchy and said that there was no observable change.

By the way, #34049 had a bad performance hit (see #rss > Significant commits to mathlib4 @ 💬 ) and I believe that the reason for this is the unfolding phenomenon that we are observing above. The proofs that Add, One, Neg etc all match up are all much longer now because Lean has to also unfold an Equiv. The unnecessary unfolding discussed above has probably been there for a while but this change exposed it.
Which declaration is the Equiv present in?

Certainly things like Equiv.addGroup should never be used without fast_instance% for exactly that reason; I see that PR has instance : Field (WithVal v) := fast_instance% (equiv v).field which looks safe enough
